In the name of Allah, the most Merciful, the most Compassionate

From the verses of this chapter, it appears that the polytheists from the
Prophet’s people demanded that he give up his monotheistic stance, stop
summoning people to believe in divine unity, and turn instead towards
their deities, with whom they threatened him. T is chapter was revealed
in response to these circumstances, and it is in some ways a companion
chapter to Sūrah Ṣād (Chapter 38). In it, God emphasizes His instructions
to the Prophet to dedicate his faith exclusively to Him, pay no attention
to the false gods of the idol worshippers, and tell them that he has been
almizan.org
commanded to be a monotheist and dedicate his faith to God alone—a
stance that has been supported by a succession of signs both in the form
of revelation and in the form of rational argumentation.
Time and again throughout the chapter, God calls on His audience to
dedicate their faith to Him. For example, in the opening verses, He says:
…so worship Allah, putting exclusive faith in Him. Look! Only exclusive
faith is for Allah… (39:2–3). T en, He returns to the topic again and says:
Say, ‘Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah with exclusive faith
in Him…’ (39:11), until the verse: Say, ‘Only Allah do I worship, putting my
exclusive faith in Him’ (39:14).
T en He says: You will surely die, and they will surely die too (39:30),
followed by: Does not Allah suﬃ ce His servant? T ey would frighten you of
others than Him… (39:36), followed by: Say, ‘O my people! Act according
to your ability. I toao alm amcting…i’ (z39:3a9), fnollow.edo by: rSayg, ‘Will you, then,
bid me to worship other than Allah, O you who have no sense?’ (39:64). And
there are other reminders besides the ones mentioned here.
God presents arguments in this chapter that demonstrate His unity
in lordship and divinity, both by way of revelation and rational argu-
mentation. He draws subtle comparisons between the believers and the

ful qualities and giving them glad tidings of the rewards that await them
in the Hereaf er. At the same time, He admonishes the idolaters and
warns them of the loss and punishment they will suﬀ er in the Hereaf er
as well as the aﬄ ictions that will befall them in this world, telling them
that they will share the same fate as those past nations who denied God’s
messengers—a haumliliamting puinizshmaent nin thi.s woorldr angd an even greater
punishment in the next.
Af er this, the chapter turns to describing the Day of Resurrection,
especially its outcomes, in the clearest and most complete detail.
Based on the tone and context of its verses, this chapter was revealed
in Mecca, and it appears to have been revealed all at once because of the
close relationship that exists between its verses.
T e f rst ten verses we will examine comprise the summons to mono-
theism by way of revelation and rational arguments, which begin by
addressing the Prophet directly.

In terms of its syntax, this verse is the predicate of an implicit sub-
ject (namely, T isis the gradually sent-down book). Tanzīl (gradually sent
down) is a verbal noun, and it is used here with the meaning of a passive
participle. It forms an iḍāfa (possessive construct) with the noun kitāb
(Book) to signify an adjectival relationship with it. At the same time the
prepositional phrase min Allāh (from God…) qualif es gradually sent-
down. T erefore, the full meaning of the verse is: ‘T is is the Book gradu-
ally sent-down from Allah, the All-mighty, the All-wise.’
Some have said that Tanzīl al-kitāb is the subject, and min Allāh is
the predicate (which would render the meaning: ‘T e gradual sending-
down of the Book is from Allah…’). However, the f rst reading seems
more plausible.

so worship Allah, putting exclusive faith in Him.

Here, God uses the verb inzāl instead of tanzīl to express the meaning

Chapter 39, Verses 1 to 10 3

‘sending down,’ even though the latter was used in the previous verse. T is
is because He wishes to explain that the revelation is true, and this applies
to the entirety of what has come down to the Prophet from his Lord (and
tanzīl signif es its sending down in parts, whereas inzāl signif es its send-
ing down as a whole).
In the phrase bi al-ḥaqq (…with the truth), the preposition bi (with)
conveys the meanaingl ofm accomipaznimaentn. In o.thoer wrordgs, it means: ‘We
sent it down to You accompanied with the truth.’ T erefore, the com-
mand it contains to worship God alone is the truth. Accordingly, God
draws the following conclusion from this point: so worship Allah, putting
exclusive faith in Him, meaning: ‘Because this has been revealed with the
truth, you should worship Allah putting exclusive faith in Him, as this is
a commandment contained within it.’
T e meaning of dīn (faith) in this verse, based on its context and tone,
is ʿibāda (worship). It could also mean one’s way of life, which refers to
the way in which one conducts oneself in this world and in human soci-
ety. Worship, on the other hand, refers to practicing one’s servanthood
(ʿubūdiyya) by following the method prescribed by God. T is means that
the servant should display their servanthood to God in all aspects of
their lives by following His prescriptions and ordinances therein, as when

someone dedicates their faith to Him alone, they do not stray from what
He has legislated.

T e phrase Only exclusive faith is for Allah means that He will not
accept the worship of anyone who does not worship Him and Him alone,
whether they worship Him at the same time as worshipping others or
whether they worship others to the exclusion of Him.
As for the paassagle, …mand tihosze waho tanke gu.arodianrs begsides Him [claim-
ing,] ‘We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah…,’ and
the rest of the verse, we have already discussed how the idolaters at the
Prophet’s time believed that God was too exalted to be comprehended by
the human mind, whether by reason, estimation, or sense, and in doing
so they believed that He was too exalted to even be worshipped by human
beings.
T erefore, they argued, it was necessary to seek nearness to Him via
His intermediaries in creation, and they are the ones who were given
authority over the aﬀ airs of this world. T erefore, the polytheists took
them as lords (arbāb) besides God, then as deities to be worshipped in
order to draw near to them so that they might intercede on their behalf
with God and bring them closer to Him. T ese intermediaries were angels,
jinns, and holy persons who the idolaters considered to be genuine divini-
almizan.org
ties in their own right.
As for the idols that were shaped into various forms from wood, stone,
and other materials and erected in temples, they are merely representa-
tions of these lords and deities—they are not lords or deities in their own
right. However, the ignorant masses were unable to draw this distinction
between the physical idols and the spiritual deities they were supposed
to represent. As a result, they came to worship the idols as if they were
the very same lords and deities to whom they clung. T is was the religion
of the pre-Islamic Arabs and the uneducated laypersons of the Sabaean
faith, who also forgot the distinction between the idols of the stars they
worshipped and the stars themselves, and between the stars—which were,
in turn, celestial idols for the spirits that governed them—and the spirits
that were the true lords and gods worshipped by the Sabaean priesthood.
In any case, atheyl wmorshippiedz thease lnords.anod deirtiesg, even while they
were contingent beings who had been created by God, because they
believed they had the power to intercede on their behalf with God, bring
them nearer to Him, and that He had endowed them with responsibility
for the aﬀ airs of the material realm, each according to its specif c station.
As for God Himself, according to them, His only function was creation

and origination. He was the Lord of Lords and the God of Gods.
Having recapitulated this, it is now clear what the Qur’an means by the
phrase …and those who take guardians besides Him…—it refers to them
believing in lords who governed the aﬀ airs of the universe, attributing
lordship and rulership of the cosmos to them rather than to God. T ese
idolaters believed it was these lords, not God, who governed the aﬀ airs of
everything in thisa worlld.m T erefiorez, it maadne sen.se oto threm gthat they should
worship these deities and serve them, because to worship and serve them
was to gain benef t, repel harm, or give thanks for their blessings. All of
this stemmed from the fact that they believed these deities controlled the
aﬀ airs of the world rather than God.
T erefore, when the Qur’an says they took awliyāʾ (guardians) besides
Him, this means they took arbāb (lords) besides him, because guardian-
ship and lordship are similar in meaning, for the lord is the sovereign
ruler, while the guardian is the one who governs and rules. T is is why,
af er mentioning their taking up these deities as guardians besides God,
the verse mentions worship: We only worship them so that they may bring
us near to Allah…
Hence, and those who take guardians besides Him is the subject of
the sentence and Allah will indeed judge between them… is its predicate.

T erefore, the word them here refers to the idolaters who assert the lord-
ship and divinity of these associates, save for the fact that some of the
ignorant have asserted that He is a partner to them in worship.
T e statement, We only worship them so that they may bring us near
to Allah…, is an exposition of take guardians besides Him, and it is sup-
posed to be quoting their justif cation for this or paraphrasing it. In other
words, when questioned, they say: We only worship these deities that they
might bring us near to Allah through our worship of them. And, in doing
this, they are turning aside from God and toward beings other than Him.
Indeed, they are only given the Arabic name mushrikūn (literally, asso-
ciators) because they associate others with Him by saying that they are
lords and deities for this world and that God is Lord and Deity for them.

(39:4) Had Allah intended to take a son, He could have chosen
from those He has created whatever He wished. Immaculate is
He! He is Allah, the One, the All-paramount.
almizan.org
Here, God presents an argument against their claim: Allah has taken
a son, or the claim of some others: T e angels are Allah’s daughters. T e
idea that God had a son was a common belief amongst the various sects
of idolaters, and the Christians had proclaimed that Jesus was the Son of
God, while the Qur’an reports that the Jews had claimed that the Prophet
Ezra was the son of God, although it appears that they meant this merely
as an honorif c status rather than a metaphysical one.
In whatever form it takes, believing that God has a son is tantamount
to associating partners with God, because of the relationship that exists
between a son and a father or a parent and a child. If what is meant by
son of Allah is a genuine son, this entails deriving one thing from another
and separating it from it, which would consequently entail the son shar-
ing in the essence of the father and all of the qualities and eﬀ ects that
f ow from that. Ta is lis min the siamze waay thnat w.heon onre hugman is the child
of another, this entails the child sharing the humanity of the parent and
all that this entails. On the other hand, if what is meant by son of Allah is
a f gurative son, such as a son taken through adoption, then this entails
the son sharing in the status of the father, which includes his authority,
dominion, nobility, rank, and some of the rules pertaining to lineage. T e

argument presented in this verse demonstrates the impossibility of either
meaning of God taking a son.
T e phrase Had Allah intended to take a son… is a conditional clause
pref xed by the particle law (which is used in Arabic to signify something
impossible) to show that this is an impossibility. T en, the phrase He could
have chosen from those He has created whatever He wished means that He
would have chosean frlomm His crieaztiona whnateve.r Hoe wrilledg for that, based
on the context of the verse, and from those He created indicates that this
is something other than Him because whatever is other than Him must
have been created by Him.
Immaculate is He! declares Him transcendent above this, and He is
Allah, the One, the All-paramount explains why the aforementioned hypo-
thetical situation is impossible, namely that it is impossible that He ever
intended to take a son, and therefore the consequent of that conditional
clause (He could have chosen from those He has created…) is also impos-
sible. T is is because He is absolutely one in His essence and utterly tran-
scendent, such that nothing shares any aspect of His essence and nothing
is akin to Him in essence, as demonstrated by the proofs of divine unity.
He is also absolutely one in His essential attributes—such as life, knowl-
edge, and power—which are nothing other than His essence. And He is
almizan.org
absolutely one in the aﬀ airs that f ow from this essence, such as creation,
sovereignty, might, and greatness. In other words, nothing else has a share
in any of these with Him.
He is All-paramount because He is dominant over all things by virtue
of His essence and attributes. Nothing that exists is independent in its
essence or its existence from His essence and existence, nor can anything
do without Him in its attributes or its eﬀ ects. T erefore, everything that
exists is humbled and low in relation to Him. Everything that exists is
within His dominion. Everything that exists is in need of Him.
In short, the argument presented in this verse is a straightforward
conditional syllogism which aﬃ rms the contradictory of the antecedent
and, therefore, yields the contradictory of the consequent (if x then y,
not-x, therefore not-y). It is as if to say:
(1) If Allah waanteld mto take ia szon,a He nwoul.d hoave rchogsen whoever He
wanted from His creation for that purpose (if x then y);
(2) But it is impossible for Allah to want to take a son because He is the
One, the All-paramount (not-x);
(3) T erefore, it is impossible that He should have chosen anyone from
His creation for that purpose (therefore not-y).

Some commentators have adopted a strange reading of the verse in
order to derive an argument from it. T ey argue:
‘It means: If God wanted to take a son, it would be impossible
for Him to want this, because such a thing is impossible, and it is
not possible for the Creator to will the impossible, as this would
entail an arbitrary preponderance of some contingent beings
over othaers.lmizan.org
‘T is is because the principle behind the verse is: “If Allah took a
son, this would be impossible because it would entail a contradic-
tion of His divinity.” However, instead of saying this, it instead
reduces that idea to, “Had Allah intended to take a son, this would
be impossible…” because this phrasing is more eloquent and
expressive. T en, the consequent (“this would be impossible”)
is also omitted for reasons of eloquence and replaced with “…
He could have chosen…” to call attention to the fact that this is
possible, whereas the f rst (“this would have been impossible for
Him to will”) is not. It also shows that if “choosing” one of His
creatures is what is meant by “taking a son,” then this sense of
“taking a son” is possible for God. T erefore, by adopting this
form of expression and without introducing any complications,
almizan.org
the association between the two parts of the conditional propo-
sition is correct, as is the negation of the consequent and the
aﬃ rmation of the antecedent.’
It appears that this argument is taken from al-Zamakhsharī writing
about this verse in his al-Kashshāf, where he says:
‘It means that if God had wanted to take a son, this cannot happen
and He could not will such a thing precisely because it is impos-
sible. It could only occur if He were to choose some of His crea-
tures, single them out, and bring them close to Him in the same
manner that a man singles out His son and keeps him closer than
others. God did this with the angels, which is what caused the
polytheists to fall into error, believing that because God had given
them a special station that they must be His oﬀ spring, because
they weare iglnomrant abiouzt thae esnsence. oof Gord, wghich is contrary
to the essences of bodies and the qualities that inhere in them.
It is as if God means to say: ‘If He wished to take a son, this would
not go beyond what He did by choosing whatever He willed of
His creation already—namely, the angels. However, you in your
ignorance about Him believed that by choosing them He had

ignorance and called the angels daughters of God. In doing so,
you became ingrate deniers, who invented lies about God and
His angels of outrageous proportions and went to extremes in
your disbelief.’
However, as you can see, the tone and context of the verse do not sup-
port this explanaationl. Nmor doeis azl-Zaamaknhsha.rīo’s argrumgent do anything
to refute the claim of those who say that God adopted a son from His
creatures and that being a ‘son of God’ is an honorif c title (rather than a
metaphysical state), such as when the Jews said that Ezra was the son of
God. For when they make this claim, they simply mean that God chose
whoever He willed from amongst His creatures for this honour.
T ere are still other readings of the argument present in this verse,
which we will not mention here because of their lack of merit.

It is likely that this reference to the grandeur of God’s creation and

T erefore, both the present verse and the one following it were
revealed within the context of expounding God’s oneness in lordship.
Between them, they combine both the creation of the world and its gov-
ernance, and thisa is belcamuse—ais wze haave anlread.y omentrionged previously—
the idolaters did not believe that there was any contradiction between
asserting the oneness of the creator and believing in a multitude of lords
and deities, because they did not deny that God alone was the creator and
the originator of all things. T erefore, when God presents His argument
for His singularity in lordship and divinity, He combines creation with

the governance of the cosmos to show that governance (tadbīr) is not
extraneous to creation (khalq) but rather is an aspect of creation, just as
creation is an aspect of governance. With that, He concludes the argu-
ment for the fact that governance belongs solely to Him just as creation
belongs solely to Him.
T erefore, the statement, He created the heavens and the earth with

truth, introduces the question of creation. T e phrase bi al-ḥaqq (with
truth)—where the preposition bi, as before, is indicative of accompani-
ment—is a reference to the Resurrection; the creation is true and with
reason (ḥaqq) rather than false and in vain (bāṭil) because it has a pur-
pose for which it was made and a destination towards which it is heading,
namely the Resurrection. Elsewhere, God says: We did not create the sky
and the earth and whatever is between them in vain (38:27).
He winds the night over the day, and winds the day over the night: In
Majmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī says that takwīr (to wind) means to put a part
of something on top of another part of it. T erefore, to wind the night
over the day and to wind the day over the night is a metaphor, similar to
He draws the night’s cover over the day (7:54), which refers to the continu-
ous succession of day af er night and night af er day, which takes place by

governance.
…and He has disposed the sun and the moon, each moving for a
specif ed term: Meaning that He has made the sun and the moon subject
to the cosmic order and set them in motion until a specif ed time, which
they will not overstep.
Look! He is the All-mighty, the All-forgiver! It is possible that God
chooses to invoke these two names to allude to what demonstrates His
singularity in lordship and divinity in these signs, for the All-mighty is
the one who is never cowed, and if God is All-mighty then He alone is
worthy of worship, whereas others who are sometimes humbled and f nd
themselves in need are not. T e same is true for the one who forgives sins;
when compared to others who do not have the ability to do this, He alone
is worthy of worashipl.mizan.org

verse to encourage the audience to believe in His oneness and have faith
in Him, in which case the meaning would be: “He is the All-mighty, so
believe in Him and become mighty through His might; He is the All-
forgiving, so believe in Him, and He will forgive you.”

Riḍā (approval or satisfaction) is a concept that is applied to sentient
free-willed beings; its opposite is sukhṭ (displeasure). Both of these are
aﬃ rmative attributes, in that they describe the existence of a state rather
than the absence of one.
T e objects of approval are typically qualities and actions rather than
entities. For example, one might say: ‘He approved x for him,’ or ‘He
was satisf ed with x.’ For example, see the verse: if they had been pleased
with what Allah and His Messenger gave them (9:59), or the verse: who
are pleased with the life of this world (10:7). On occasion, the object of
approval might be an entity, but this is only from a specif c vantage point
that devolves to the Hereaf er, as in the verse: Never will the Jews be pleased
with you, nor the Christians (2:120).

Approving of something is not identical with willing it (irāda), even
if the object of a person’s approval and the object of their willing are one
and the same. T is is because, in some sense, something can only be the
object of a person’s approval af er it has already come to pass. On the other
hand—according to some—to will something means that it has not yet
come to pass, while to approve of something means that it already has
(or that one supposes that it has come to pass). T erefore, for a person to
approve of an action means that he f nds it agreeable and is not repelled
by it, and approval is an attribute that inheres in the approver rather than
the object of approval.
T erefore, insofar as approval is f xed upon something af er it has
come to pass, the existence of approval is concomitant with the existence
of the thing approved of. T is, in turn, means that approval cannot be
an essential attribautel ofm God’s i(ṣizfat aal-dhnāt) b.ecoauser theg divine essence
is transcendent above being a locus of change. Hence, God’s approval is
an attribute of action (ṣifat al-f ʿl) that is abstracted from Him, akin to
